title: "Dealing with spatio-temporal autocorrelation"

```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(DHARMa)
library(sdmTMB)
library(lmtest)
library(performance)
library(modelbased)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(car)
library(scales)
```

## What happens when you have both spatial AND temporal autocorrelation?

So far, we've dealt with problems that consider only spatial autocorrelation. But autocorrelation can result from repeated measurements, also. How we deal with these situations is tricky and, to some extent, context dependent. Here, we'll work through an example that illustrates the sorts of things you should be thinking about when approaching this type of problem. But we'll caution you that other data sets will raise other sorts of problems.


## Giant kelp and marine heatwave

Our example is based on a slightly modified version of the data used in [Arafeh Dalmau et al. (2025) Marine heatwaves drive range contraction and alternative states of kelp forests at the warm limit of their distribution](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.17.682914v1.full). The study area comprises the distribution of giant-kelp forests along the Pacific coastline of Mexico, extending southwards from the US border to the southern distribution limit of giant kelp in the northern hemisphere at Punta Prieta. The region can be divided into two sub-regions: northern Baja California (32.53--29.73°N), characterized by relatively cooler upwelled waters; and the warmer central Baja California (29.73--27°N). 

We focus on the 18-year period 2006--2023, inclusive, which is centred on a series of exceptional marine heatwaves during 2015--2016 (the phenomenon known as "The Blob"). We are interested in finding out whether the marine heatwaves (MHWs) impacted giant kelp populations and if so, whether any effects were consistent in northern and central Baja California.

To answer this question, we collated time series of satellite-based estimates of kelp area, measured at 30-m grid resolution by three Landsat sensors, then aggregated estimates onto a 0.25º grid. This provides annual (`year`) estimates of kelp cover (`area`; ha) for each of 37 coastal 0.25º grid squares (`pixelid`, with coordinates `lon` and `lat`). Observations north of 29.73°N are classified as belonging to the "north" `region`, with the rest being "central", and observations from 2014 or earlier are considered to belong to the `period` "before" the MHWs started, with the rest being "after".

Let's load up the packages we'll need in this session, retrieve the data for this analysis and plot the study area:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(DHARMa)
library(sdmTMB)
library(lmtest)
library(performance)
library(modelbased)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(car)
library(scales)
```

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Get the data
 df <- read_csv("data/blob_kelp.csv") %>% # Read in the data
    filter(year == 2006) %>% # Get just the first year, so that we don't have replicated 0.25º grid squares
    dplyr::select(pixelid, lon, lat, region) # Get just the coordinates of the 0.25º grid squares, and their identities

# Build a land polygon
  sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE) # Switches off the use of the Google S2 spherical geometry library within the sf package and reverts to using the GEOS library for geometric operations. 
  bbox <- ext(-118, -112, 26.75, 33) # A rough bounding box for the study area
  land <- ne_countries(scale = 50) %>% # A medium-resolution database of country polygons
    st_crop(bbox) %>% # Cropped to our bounding box
    st_geometry() # Retain only the geometries, not any of the other descriptors

# Build a plot    
  ggplot() + 
    geom_sf(data = land, fill = "wheat") + # Plot the land and colour it in
    geom_tile(data = df, aes(lon, lat, fill = region), # Add equal-sized tiles for the coordinates
              alpha = .2, # Transparent
              colour = "black", # With black outlines
              show.legend = FALSE) + # No legend
    geom_text(data = df, aes(lon, lat, label = pixelid), # Add pixelid labels
              size = 2) + # Make them readable
    geom_hline(yintercept = 29.72, # A horizontal line separating north and central regions
               colour = "red", # Make it red
               lty = "dashed") + # Make it dashed
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "cadetblue4"), # Colour the grid squares by weatther they are in the northern or southern sub-region
      na.value = "transparent") + # Set NAs to be transparent
    labs(x = "", y = "") + # No x- or y-axis labels
    theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "lightblue", color = NA)) + # Make the sea blue
    ylim(c(27.05, 32.7)) + # Clip the figure to avoid polygon bounds being visible
    xlim(c(-117.5, -112.5)) # Clip the figure to avoid polygon bounds being visible
```
We can see that some grid squares are contiguous with others, but there are also some fairly large spatial breaks among grid squares. We would therefore expect grid squares that are closer together to be more similar to each other than those that are far apart---i.e., we expect these data to contain some spatial autocorrelation. In this case, we won't consider these as aerial spatial data, but will rather use their centroids to define spatial associations. We've seen this before, and we know how to deal with it. But in this case, we *also* have observations from each grid square for consecutive years in a long sequence, which means that we also need to consider temporal autocorrelation.

## Inspect the time series

Let's start our analysis by just plotting the time series.

```{r}
dat <- read_csv("data/blob_kelp.csv") %>% 
  mutate(across(where(is.character), factor), # Make character variables into factors
         pixelid = factor(pixelid), # Convert this one manually, because it is a number, not a character
         region = fct_relevel(region, "north"), # Make "north" the first factor level
         period = fct_relevel(period, "before")) %>% # Make "before" the first factor level 
  add_utm_columns(ll_names = c("lon", "lat")) # Add columns of UTM coordinates...we'll need this later

col_pal <- c(c("cadetblue4", "darkorange")) # The same colour palette as we used in the map
ggplot(dat) +
  geom_line(aes(x = year, y = area, colour = region)) + # Plot the time series, coloured by region
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2014.5, # A vertical line to indicate the separation of "before" and "after" the onset of the MHWs
             linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "red") +
  labs(colour = "Region", # Sort out axis and legend labels
       x = "",
       y = "Areal coverage of kelp (ha)") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col_pal) + # Set the colour palette
  facet_wrap(vars(pixelid)) + # Make a separate panel for each time series
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", # Put legend at the bottom
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 5)) # Make x-axis text small enough to prevent overlap
```

We can see from this plot, we can see that there is a large amount of variation in kelp cover, both through time and among grid squares. Generally, there seems to be more kelp before the MHWs hit than after, with perhaps more of a persistent suppression of kelp in the central `region`, but it remains questionable whether this effect is statistically detectable, given the noise in the data.

## Building the spatial mesh

We'll be using `sdmTMB` again here, so we'll start by building our spatial mesh:

```{r}
mesh <- make_mesh(dat, xy_cols = c("X", "Y"), cutoff = 10)
plot(mesh)
```

## A simple mixed-effects model without consideration of spatial or temporal autocorrelation

Before we knew about autocorrelation, we might have started this analysis with a model of kelp `area` as a function of `region`, `period`, their interaction and a random grouping effect for `pixelid`. This model considers observations for each grid square to be fully independent of each other across time and space. Yes, we know that potentially introduces pseudoreplication (i.e., overestimating the number of degrees of freedom in the analysis), but let's start here, anyway, for the sake of illustration:

```{r}
m1 <- sdmTMB(area ~ region * period +
               (1 | pixelid),
             mesh = mesh,
             spatial = "off",
             data = dat,
             family = tweedie())
```

Note that we have used the Tweedie distribution here, with its canonical log link function. The Tweedie distribution is extremely useful when your response data comprises only zeros and positive numbers, especially where the distribution of those response data might be skewed---so as an ecologist, it is very good to have the Tweedie distribution in your toolkit.

Let's check the significance of the model terms:

```{r}
#| warning: false
Anova(m1)
```

It seems as if all terms are highly significant, so there is an effect of both `region` and `period`, with the effect of `period` depending on the `region` considered.

We can illustrate this with a plot:

```{r}
# Build a prediction tibble
  new_dat <- expand_grid(region = levels(dat$region),
                         period = levels(dat$period), # A tibble with two variables containing all possible combinations of region and period 
                         year = min(dat$year)) # We'll add a single value for year, here, even though we're not using it yet

# Predict values from our model for this prediction tibble
  preds1 <- estimate_expectation(m1, new_dat) %>% 
    tibble()

# Plot the results
  ggplot() +
    geom_errorbar(data = preds1,
                  aes(x = period, ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high, colour = region),
                  width = .05,
                  linewidth = 1,
                  position = position_dodge(.3)) +
    geom_point(data = preds1,
               aes(x = period, y = Predicted, colour = region),
               position = position_dodge(.3),
               size = 3) +
    labs(colour = "Region",
         y = "Areal coverage of kelp ± 95% confidence (ha)",
         x = "Timing relative to the onset of MHWs") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = col_pal)
```

This result suggests that there are strongly significant differences in kelp coverage for each combination of `period` and `region`, with clear indications that there is less kelp in central regions and that kelp coverage declined sharply with the onset of MHWs, perhaps more so (in absolute terms) in the northern than in the central "region`.

What do the model diagnostics look like?

```{r}
# A function for plotting residuals from sdmTMB models
sdmTMB_residuals <- function(model, nsim = 1000, plot = TRUE) {
  set.seed(123456) # Set the random seed so that we get the same results for randomisations
  sims <- simulate({{model}}, nsim = nsim, type = "mle-mvn") # We can't use DHARMa residuals "As is" with sdmTMB
  res <- dharma_residuals({{model}}, simulated_response = sims, integerResponse = TRUE, return_DHARMa = TRUE)
  if(plot != TRUE) {
    return(res)
    } else {
      plot(res)
      }
  }

# Deploy the function
sdmTMB_residuals(m1)
```
These diagnostics aren't terrible, although there are some indications that residuals are not homoscedastic.

But are our observations really independent---i.e., are we missing any autocorrelation?

## Adding spatial autocorrelation

Since we anticipate that kelp cover in grid squares closer to each other would be more similar than would be the case among distant grid squares, let's account for spatial autocorrelation in our model:


```{r}
#| cache: true
#| warning: false
m2 <- sdmTMB(area ~ region * period,
             mesh = mesh,
             spatial = "on", # Switch on the random spatial mesh
             data = dat,
             family = tweedie())
Anova(m2)
```

It seems as if all terms remain highly significant.

Let's plot the predictions:

```{r}
# Predict values from our model for this prediction tibble
  preds2 <- estimate_expectation(m2, new_dat) %>% 
    tibble()

# Plot the results
  ggplot(preds2) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(x = period, ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high, colour = region),
                  width = .05,
                  linewidth = 1,
                  position = position_dodge(.3)) +
    geom_point(aes(x = period, y = Predicted, colour = region),
               position = position_dodge(.3),
               size = 3) +
    labs(colour = "Region",
         y = "Areal coverage of kelp ± 95% confidence (ha)",
         x = "Timing relative to the onset of MHWs") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = col_pal)
```

The results look quite similar, so let's check the diagnostics:

```{r}
sdmTMB_residuals(m2)
```
These diagnostics aren't much different from those for our simpler model. But they're still not great. Perhaps adding temporal autocorrelation will help?

## A model with both spatial and temporal autocorrelation

### Let's start with temporal autocorrelation as AR1

For time series that are stationary---i.e., time series that fluctuate around some long-term mean, rather than following some long-term trend---we generally specify temporal autocorrelation as autoregressive, often of order 1 ("AR1"). This form of autocorrelation assumes a "memory" (dependence) that goes no further back than the previous observation.

Let's check our time series for the presence of significant temporal autocorrelation at lag 1. The simplest way is with the Durbin-Watson test:

```{r}
# Run a Durbin-Watson test for each time series, each time extracting just the p-value from the test
dat %>% 
  arrange(year) %>%  # Sort by year to ensure that the data are ordered in time
  group_by(pixelid) %>% # Group by pixel to ensure that we work one time series at a time
  summarise(p = dwtest(area ~ 1) %>% pluck("p.value")) %>% # For each time series, run the test and extract the p-value
  mutate(significance = ifelse(p <= 0.05, "***significant***", "non-significant")) %>% # Make a new column to make it easier to spot significant results
  print(n = nrow(.)) # Print all rows
```

It seems like there is significant AR1 temporal autocorrelation in almost half of the time series. So let's try to account for it.

```{r}
#| cache: true
#| warning: false
m3 <- sdmTMB(area ~ region * period +
             (1 | pixelid),
             mesh = mesh,
             spatial = "on",
             time = "year", # Specify that year controls for time
             spatiotemporal = "ar1", # Specify autoregressive correlation of order 1
             data = dat,
             family = tweedie())
Anova(m3)
```

All model terms remain significant. But what about the residuals?

```{r}
sdmTMB_residuals(m3)
```

These residuals are a substantial improvement. The QQ plot is pretty neat, and there are some indications of the trends for residuals at the three quartiles to flatten somewhat across the centre of the range of predictions---OK, they're not flat, and those for the thrid quartile are still increasing steeply, but "better" is better, not perfect.

Let's plot the result for the sake of comparison:

```{r}
# Predict values from our model for this prediction tibble
  preds3 <- estimate_expectation(m3, new_dat) %>% 
    tibble()

# Plot the results
  ggplot(preds3) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(x = period, ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high, colour = region),
                  width = .05,
                  linewidth = 1,
                  position = position_dodge(.3)) +
    geom_point(aes(x = period, y = Predicted, colour = region),
               position = position_dodge(.3),
               size = 3) +
    labs(colour = "Region",
         y = "Areal coverage of kelp ± 95% confidence (ha)",
         x = "Timing relative to the onset of MHWs") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = col_pal)
```

Now that we have accounted for potential correlation among observations within each time series, the error bars have spread considerably. This is a clear indication that estimation is now based on fewer degrees of freedom---which is what we wanted the routine to do, because there are fewer truly independent observations in each time series. 

On the basis of this plot, it seems like there is little difference in kelp cover between regions before the initiation of MHWs, that kelp cover declines in both subregions after the initiation of MHWs, and that there is less kelp in central than the northern region after the MHWs.

But our original plot of time series didn't suggest that they were stationary, so would some other form of temporal autocorrelation do better?

### Temporal autocorrelation as a random walk

Where the data has "memory" (dependence) but little clear tendency to return to a fixed central value, it can be more appropriate to model temporal autocorrelation as a random walk. So let's give that a crack:

```{r}
#| cache: true
#| warning: false
m4 <- sdmTMB(area ~ region * period +
               (1 | pixelid),
             mesh = mesh,
             spatial = "on",
             time = "year", # Specify that year controls for time
             spatiotemporal = "rw", # Specify random walk for temporal autocorrelation
             data = dat,
             family = tweedie())
Anova(m4)
```
We're starting to see a shift in the significance of model terms, now. But remember that we shouldn't be interpreting main effects when a significant interaction is present. So let's plot the output and interpret that, instead.

```{r}
# Predict values from our model for this prediction tibble
  preds4 <- estimate_expectation(m4, new_dat) %>% 
    tibble()

# Plot the results
  ggplot(preds4) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(x = period, ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high, colour = region),
                  width = .05,
                  linewidth = 1,
                  position = position_dodge(.3)) +
    geom_point(aes(x = period, y = Predicted, colour = region),
               position = position_dodge(.3),
               size = 3) +
    labs(colour = "Region",
         y = "Areal coverage of kelp ± 95% confidence (ha)",
         x = "Timing relative to the onset of MHWs") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = col_pal)
```
It seems as if the confidence bands are a little tighter, but that overall interpretation isn't much different.

What about the diagnostics?

```{r}
sdmTMB_residuals(m4)
```

These are pretty good. Specifically, we can see further "flattening" of the curves fitted to the quantiles of the residuals. Yes, there seems to be an issue with over-estimating large values, but for most of the observations, this result is pretty good.

Which model is best?

```{r}
compare_performance(m1, m2, m3, m4)
```
It seems as if our model with random walk temporal autocorrelation is preferred, both in terms of AIC and BIC. Since the residuals for this model are also better than for any of our previous candidate models, we'll stop here.

### A last check of the residuals using the partial autocorrelation function

The Partial Autocorrelation Function (`pacf`) measures the direct correlation between a time series and versions of itself at increasing lags, without the influence of intermediate lags. We're looking for significant autocorrelations (bars that extend beyond the horizontal dashed red lines) and, specifically, consistent patterns in these significant autocorrelations.

To make it easier to repeat these plots, we build a plotting function, then deploy it:

```{r}
plot_pacf_by_group <- function(model, data, time_var, grouping_var) {
df <- data %>% 
  mutate(residuals = sdmTMB_residuals(model, plot = FALSE) %>% 
           pluck("scaledResiduals")) %>%  # Append the residuals from the model to the data
  arrange({{time_var}}) %>% 
  group_by({{grouping_var}}) %>% # Group by pixelid (i.e., by time series)
  summarise(PACF = list(pacf(residuals, plot = FALSE) %>% # For each time series, extract the pacf stats
                          pluck("acf")), # Retaining ONLY the autocorrelation function values
            n = n()) %>% # Compute the number of observations by group
  unnest(cols = PACF) %>%  # Spread the nested tibbles created from the summarise function
  group_by({{grouping_var}}) %>% 
  mutate(lag = row_number()) %>% # Add lags by group
  ungroup()
ggplot() +
  geom_col(data = df, # Column graphs
           aes(x = lag, y = PACF),  # pacf by lag
           fill = "skyblue") +
  facet_wrap(vars({{grouping_var}})) + # Creates separate panels for each ID
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + # Horizontal line at zero (i.e., no autocorrelation)
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(1.96, -1.96)/df %>% pull(n) %>% min() %>% sqrt(), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") + # Approx confidence limits
  labs(x = "Lag", y = "Partial Autocorrelation") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = breaks_width(2)) +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 5)) # Make x-axis text small enough to prevent overlap
  }  
  
plot_pacf_by_group(model = m4, 
                   data = dat, 
                   time_var = year, 
                   grouping_var = pixelid)
```

There are relatively few significant autocorrelations in the individual time series, and no discernible patterns, so although our model has not entirely eliminated all traces of autocorrelation, it seems to have done a reasonable job.

We can use a Durbin-Watson test to confirm that few time series or model residuals retain significant autocorrelation at lag 1:

```{r}
dat %>% 
  mutate(residuals = sdmTMB_residuals(m4, plot = FALSE) %>% 
           pluck("scaledResiduals")) %>% 
  group_by(pixelid) %>% 
  summarise(p = dwtest(residuals ~ 1) %>% pluck("p.value")) %>%
  mutate(significance_p = ifelse(p <= 0.05, "***significant***", "non-significant")) %>% 
  print(n = nrow(.))
```

The residuals of only 3 time series retain autocorrelation at lag 1 (proibably none, if you adjust for multiple comparisons), which is a good sign. It seems as if we've done about as well as we can.

## Take-aways

Modelling spatial and temporal autocorrelation sounds difficult, and it *can* be tricky, but we have reasonably simple tools that we can help. Of course, when things get messy, as they often do in ecology, we need to dig deeper, but hopefully this brief overview is enough to prepare you for that ordeal 😉.

### R books and web material

There are plenty of good books out there (too many to choose from in
fact). For the content we covered today, some good resources are:

-   [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/){target="_blank"}, for
    data wrangling mainly

-   [R Graphics
    Cookbook](http://www.cookbook-r.com/Graphs/){target="_blank"}, for
    `ggplot` and free on the web

-   [Spatial Data
    Science](https://r-spatial.org/book/){target="_blank"}, for `sf` and
    more

-   [Geocomputation in
    R](https://geocompr.robinlovelace.net/){target="_blank"}, free on
    the web

-   [Spatial Statistics for Data
    Science](https://www.paulamoraga.com/book-spatial/index.html){target="_blank"},
    for spatial statistics

-   The classic text for GAMs is [Generalized Additive Models: An
    Introduction with
    R](https://www.routledge.com/Generalized-Additive-Models-An-Introduction-with-R-Second-Edition/Wood/p/book/9781498728331){target="_blank"}.
    This has a very technical treatment of GAMs, but also an extensive
    section with practical examples, including spatial ones.

-   If you want to learn new tricks, or stay up-to-date with the latest
    packages, the blog aggregator
    [R-Bloggers](https://www.r-bloggers.com/){target="_blank"} has a
    non-step feed of R blogs from all over the world and all
    disciplines, including [Nicholas Clark's
    blog](https://ecogambler.netlify.app/blog/){target="_blank"}, [Chris
    Brown's
    blog](http://www.seascapemodels.org/bluecology_blog.html){target="_blank"}
    and [Gavin Simpson's
    blog](https://fromthebottomoftheheap.net/){target="_blank"}

If you prefer to have a printed guide, another tactic is to web search
your favourite package and "cheatsheet".
